explanation: Because the CPython Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) permits only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time, multithreading is only beneficial for I/O-bound tasks (network requests, DB queries). CPU-bound data transformations (JSON parsing, regex, compression) require multiprocessing or ProcessPoolExecutor to utilize all available CPU cores.
keyPoints: Threading shares address space; ideal for I/O concurrency
Multiprocessing bypasses GIL by spawning separate OS processes
Inter-process communication requires pickle serialization or shared memory

definition: Decorators are higher-order functions that dynamically wrap and extend the behavior of another function or method without altering its source code.
explanation: In enterprise data engineering, decorators are the standard mechanism for cross-cutting concerns: automated exponential backoff retries on network failures, distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry), execution timing/metrics, caching (@functools.lru_cache), and role-based authentication.
keyPoints: Higher-order function wrapping another callable using @syntax
Standard for retries, telemetry logging, performance timing, and caching
Preserves function metadata using functools.wraps

definition: The Global Interpreter Lock is a mutual exclusion lock used by CPython to prevent multiple native OS threads from executing Python bytecode simultaneously, protecting internal memory reference counts.
explanation: CPython's memory manager relies on reference counting, which is not thread-safe without atomic locks on every reference change. The GIL solves this with a single global lock. In data systems, native C/Rust extensions (NumPy, Polars, PyArrow, DuckDB) explicitly release the GIL (Py_BEGIN_ALLOW_THREADS) before executing heavy compute, enabling true multi-core parallel execution.
keyPoints: Serializes bytecode execution to protect CPython reference counting
Prevents multi-threaded CPU scaling in pure Python code
Third-party C/Rust extensions release the GIL for full multi-core performance

definition: Polars LazyFrame defers DataFrame computations into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) that undergoes logical optimization (predicate and projection pushdown) prior to vectorized execution.
explanation: Unlike Pandas which executes eagerly and materializes intermediate DataFrames into RAM, Polars LazyFrame builds an execution plan. The Polars optimizer pushes filters down directly to the Parquet scanner (predicate pushdown), discards unused columns (projection pushdown), and processes data in streaming chunks, enabling datasets larger than RAM to be processed seamlessly.
keyPoints: Builds optimized logical execution graph before touching storage
Predicate & projection pushdown minimizes disk I/O and RAM allocation
Written in Rust with multi-threaded parallel SIMD execution

definition: Apache Arrow is a standardized columnar in-memory format that enables zero-copy sharing of data arrays between different execution engines without serialization overhead.
explanation: Traditional data interchange between Python, Spark, and DuckDB requires costly serialization to CSV or JSON and deserialization back into memory. Arrow defines an immutable, SIMD-aligned columnar layout in shared memory. Systems like PySpark (via PyArrow) transfer DataFrames to Python workers with zero copying or IPC serialization penalty.
keyPoints: Language-independent columnar in-memory format specification
Zero-copy shared memory IPC between Python, C++, Rust, and Spark
Native support for chunked arrays, dictionaries, and nested data structures

term: Python AsyncIO Event Loop & Non-Blocking I/O
definition: AsyncIO provides single-threaded concurrent execution using cooperative multitasking managed by an event loop, scheduling coroutines using async and await keywords.
explanation: When ingesting data from thousands of REST API endpoints, WebSockets, or cloud blob storage, synchronous requests block worker threads. AsyncIO leverages OS primitives (epoll/kqueue) to handle tens of thousands of concurrent network connections on a single CPU core without thread context-switching overhead.
keyPoints: Single-threaded cooperative concurrency driven by an OS event loop
Eliminates thread context-switching overhead for massive network concurrency
Requires non-blocking async libraries (aiohttp, httpx, asyncpg)

definition: CPython manages memory through reference counting supplemented by a cyclic generational garbage collector (Generations 0, 1, and 2) and the PyMalloc sub-allocator for small objects.
explanation: In Petabyte-scale Python worker microservices, cyclic references prevent memory reclamation by reference counts alone, causing generational GC pauses. Architects use tracemalloc and objgraph to profile heap allocations, invoke gc.freeze() in pre-forked worker pools (e.g. Celery/Gunicorn) to leverage Linux Copy-On-Write (COW), and bypass the allocator using memoryview and ctypes for raw buffers.
keyPoints: Dual memory model: reference counting + 3-generation cyclic GC
gc.freeze() preserves Copy-On-Write memory across forked worker pools
tracemalloc captures source-level heap allocations and memory leaks

term: High-Throughput Polyglot Arrow IPC & Flight Architecture
definition: Arrow Flight is a high-performance RPC framework built on gRPC and Arrow columnar data, designed specifically for parallel stream transfer of large tabular datasets across distributed cluster nodes.
explanation: Architecting microservices that transfer multi-gigabyte DataFrames over standard REST/JSON creates 90%+ CPU waste in serialization. Arrow Flight transfers memory-mapped Arrow record batches directly over TCP without translation, supporting distributed parallel streams where clients read multiple stream partitions simultaneously from different cluster nodes.
keyPoints: Zero-serialization RPC framework optimized for big data transport
Outperforms REST/ODBC/JDBC by 10x-100x for large record batch transfers
Enables federated query engines to exchange partitions in parallel

term: Rust PyO3 Extension Architecture for Data Pipelines
definition: PyO3 provides Rust bindings for Python, allowing developers to write native Rust extension modules that compile into shared libraries (.so / .pyd) callable directly from Python code.
explanation: When core pipeline bottlenecks (e.g., custom binary parsing, financial trade simulations, geo-spatial hashing) saturate Python CPU cores, architects write high-performance native extensions in Rust with PyO3 and Maturin. Rust guarantees memory safety without garbage collection, enables fearless Rayon thread parallelism with GIL release, and exposes clean Python APIs.
keyPoints: Compiles memory-safe native Rust code into native Python extension modules
Releases the GIL to leverage Rayon multi-threaded parallelism across all CPU cores
Powers modern data tools including Polars, Ruff, and Pydantic-Core

term: Distributed Python Runtimes: Ray vs PySpark Architecture
definition: Ray is an asynchronous distributed actor and task execution framework designed for Python-native distributed computing, contrasting with PySpark's JVM-centric BSP (Bulk Synchronous Parallel) execution model.
explanation: While PySpark excels at SQL, tabular lakehouse transforms, and massive batch shuffles, its JVM-Python inter-process communication overhead and rigid DAG barrier synchronization create friction for dynamic ML training, reinforcement learning, and fine-grained agent loops. Ray provides native shared-memory object storage (Plasma), sub-millisecond task scheduling, and stateful actor clusters.
keyPoints: Ray features distributed actors, tasks, and Plasma shared memory
PySpark uses JVM workers and Bulk Synchronous Parallel execution plans
Architectural choice: Spark for data lakehouse ETL; Ray for ML/AI workloads
